analysis.one_liner: Ranks counties by toxic chemical releases, inspects facilities in the worst 100, and funds community health studies.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on June 24, 1993 and never advanced; it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Environmental Justice Act of 1993 would have required the EPA to rank every county by the total weight of toxic chemicals released, naming the worst 100 as 'Environmental High Impact Areas.' Facilities in those areas would have faced inspections at least every two years, and the Department of Health and Human Services would have studied whether residents there suffer more cancer, birth defects, infant mortality, and respiratory disease than people elsewhere. If significant harm was found, the bill required the President to propose new rules, and barred new federal permits for facilities unless they cut the chemicals found to be causing that harm. It also offered small grants so residents of affected areas could hire technical help and take part in the process.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in the 100 counties with the heaviest toxic chemical releases — communities that the bill's findings said are disproportionately low-income and minority — would gain mandatory inspections of nearby polluting facilities, a federally funded health study of their exposure, and small grants (up to $50,000, with a possible waiver of the 20% local match) to hire their own experts and participate [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of the most polluted counties

how_it_helps.text: EPA must publish a ranked list of toxic releases by county and designate the top 100 as Environmental High Impact Areas, giving residents and officials an objective map of who is most exposed [S2][S3].
EPA and the Labor Department must inspect every toxic chemical facility in those areas at least every two years, rather than leaving compliance checks to chance [S2][S3].

HHS must report on whether people in those areas suffer more cancer, birth deformities, infant mortality, and respiratory disease than residents of other counties, and the President must propose remedies if significant harm is found [S2][S3].

If significant adverse health impacts are confirmed, new or modified facilities in those areas must produce a net reduction in the chemicals found to be causing the harm as a condition of any federal permit [S2][S3].

Residents threatened by toxic releases can receive grants up to $50,000 for technical assistance and to take part in the public process, with a 20% local share that can be waived for financial need [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical, hazardous waste, and other industrial facilities in the worst 100 counties would bear the cost of frequent inspections, potential emissions fees or release restrictions, and a requirement to cut pollution as a condition of new or modified permits. Reporting facilities more broadly could face an expanded disclosure list if the health report triggered new requirements [S2][S3]. The bill's grants and studies also depend on federal appropriations [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial facilities in highly polluted counties

drawbacks.text: The bill does not itself cut toxic releases anywhere; it first builds a data list and a health study, and only if the study finds significant adverse impacts does the President propose changes and permit conditions tighten — so relief for residents would be slow and dependent on agency follow-through [S2][S3].

Ranking by 'total weight' of toxic releases could be a blunt measure, and the bill directs EPA to adjust for toxicity 'whenever possible,' suggesting imperfect data quality would affect which counties land in the top 100 [S3].

Mandatory inspections of every facility in the top 100 counties at least every two years, plus new fees and permit conditions, impose real compliance costs on industry in those areas, which supporters of the bill would need to weigh against the health findings the bill itself required first [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill invests most of its effort in information — a ranked list, a health study, inspections — before mandating any specific reduction, which makes it a cautious bill rather than a sweeping one. Its main strength is giving residents of heavily polluted, disproportionately low-income and minority communities the data, inspections, and small grants to force attention on their exposure. Its weakness is that actual cleanup is deferred: no chemical is reduced unless the government completes its study, finds significant harm, and the President proposes and agencies adopt remedies. Industry compliance costs are real but targeted at the worst 100 counties only.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Max Baucus introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1993 on June 24, 1993, joined by Sens. Moseley-Braun and Campbell [S1][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearings, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial facilities in the counties with the heaviest toxic releases avoided the mandated inspections, potential fees, and permit requirements, and residents of those counties got no new federal health study or assistance.

for.name: Sen. Max Baucus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1993 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 24, 1993 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three Senate supporters were Democrats and the bill never reached a vote, so no recorded vote shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: Facilities in the 100 worst counties would face inspections at least every two years, possible emissions fees or release restrictions, and a net-reduction requirement on new or modified permits. Their cost is the public health protection residents of those counties would gain.
Facilities that generate, treat, store, or dispose of hazardous waste are covered as toxic chemical facilities and subject to the same inspection and permit rules.

industries.industry: Environmental and health data and technical consulting services
industries.note: The bill funds federal health studies and up to $50,000 grants per area for residents to obtain technical assistance, creating work for experts assisting affected communities.
